title: The Incomparability of the Son
english: They think that the intelligible things are made similar to the flows of matter. For the heavenly things surpass all mind and all thought, while the earthly and lowly things are subject to becoming and passing away in time. But especially, [the Son] was begotten without beginning, co-existing and co-working with his own true Father, like light to the solar disk. And the fact that God, Lord, Holy, Creator, Imperishable, Life, Light, and all that the Father is, exists, is testified from the Scriptures. And it is more fitting to have the similar and equal from the many than the dissimilar from the one. How is it that Adam and Eve, not having been begotten and not having had a father, have become equal in nature to those from them? Or what simple comparison have they made, saying the 'dissimilar,' or how, having measured, have they arrived at the 'greater and larger'? For Scripture neither defines the holy and unbegotten, one and indivisible Trinity by nature, nor again distinguishes for it the first and the second. But these two things are being made manifest: that the greater is not in any way heterousios, and that the comparative terms apply to those of the same substance, not to those of different substance. Nor would one say it is opportune even by imposition, not even concerning the 'incomparable and greater.' Not according to size or any volume; for the God Word has withdrawn from all magnitude and simplicity, and from all bulk, composition, and form, just as the Father and his Holy Spirit, being contained by nothing, yet containing all. Because he is also the beginning of all magnitudes, like a creator. For where is size in the most sublime, supersubstantial, and superior hypostases? Nor even according to the unbegotten. For he co-exists with the Father as an 'emanation of his glory' and not having God before him. For he indeed says: 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1). And God the Creator is not measured by time relative to the creation. Since it is necessary for them to require—which is a dangerous thought to conceive—a time prior to the unbegotten and incomprehensible God and Father, and thus to compare. But men are accustomed to call 'greater' those who have preceded in time in generation, according to Isaac who ordains: 'the greater shall serve the less.' Nor as a cause. [Text ends abruptly]
He is not the cause of it. For the only-begotten Son was shown to be without beginning, since he is greater than both himself and us in the same way, which would be impossible to say or even to hear.

Nor [is he greater] according to essence and similarity. For from him it is said, 'as the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth' (John 1:14), and as 'the character of the hypostasis,' being a character toward all things, and as 'the image of God,' whom 'he who has seen has seen the Father' (John 14:9). 'For in him dwells all the fullness of deity' (Colossians 2:9). And this is drawn out by the testimony of 'let us make man in our image and according to our likeness' (Genesis 1:26).

Nor [is he greater] according to a distinction of quality, since the divine and unsearchable hypostases are not qualities; for quality belongs to bodies, but they are incorporeal and intellectual. But it is not even possible to think about them [in terms of comparison], as if the beautiful were more beautiful than the lovely, similarly to the voice of Paul speaking concerning another: 'But now these three remain, faith, hope, love; but the greatest of these is love' (1 Corinthians 13:13). For through the distinction toward virtue, he gained the 'greater' through love. For, he says, having loved, we believe, and having believed, we hope to reign with Christ.

For if the 'one God' (1 Corinthians 8:6) and 'that you may become partakers of the divine nature' (2 Peter 1:4) and not of natures, is true, and it has been demonstrated that the whole thing is one, I say: the deity. Nor [is he greater] according to equality, because it is written that the Son is 'God,' great and 'over all' (Ephesians 1:22), 'making himself equal to the Father' (Philippians 2:6) and 'swearing by himself, since he has no greater' (Hebrews 6:13).

Nor [is he greater] according to power. For it is written: 'the power of God and the wisdom of God' (1 Corinthians 1:24), and 'all things as the Father does, the Son also does in the same way' (John 14:10). Nor [is he greater] according to glory or any honor. 'For if we had known,' he says, 'we would not have crucified the Lord of glory' (1 Corinthians 2:8). And it is the will of the Father, according to John, 'that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father' (John 5:23).

According to what, then, remains the greater and the dissimilar? As it was shown, according to nothing. And indeed the apostle, preventing the impious suppositions of heretics regarding the only-begotten Son and God, yet [preventing] the identity of nature toward his Father, and furthermore proclaiming the without-beginning, having written as was said above: 'who being the radiance of the glory of the Father' (Hebrews 1:3) brought forth: 'and the character of his hypostasis.'
And

title: The distinction between image and essence
english: Again, regarding the Colossians and the Hebrews, it is written: 'who is the image of the invisible God' (Col 1:15). And in the Gospel according to John, the Son, presenting his own essence to be stamped with a Fatherly character, said: 'for this God the Father has stamped' (John 5:23).

This makes manifest the co-existence of the seal with the archetype, being of like-nature, and in itself showing perfectly and truly the unity of nature of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For the seal, just like the character, signifies that which is similar and undefiled.

Since it is a time to speak, and it is not improper or incomparable to have the Father [as the archetype], even if he is being imaged and characterized by a created and dissimilar thing. These divine things, not understanding correctly the words of unsearchable interpretation, but twisting them and contending with human thoughts against the words of God, say: 'another God and another image of God, just as another man and another image of a man.'

And in a certain way they represent the living and active God-Logos as a motionless image. But in essence and in every respect, he is an unerring and sovereign image of the Father, and not according to form and shape, like a statue carved or sculpted, breathless and not self-moving, nor according to kind and color, like an artificial and imitative silent image. For these things do not even according to nature, nor indeed in all other respects, manifest the Prototype.

For indeed the Son is an image of his own Father's essence of a man; but it happens to deviate in age or kind or mind or power or dignity or related things or something else. But the God-Logos unerringly and precisely images in all respects the simple, undivided, and unlike Fatherly divinity, naturally and sovereignly.

For it is not possible to think, as if he were an image of God according to something and deviates from something; nor indeed does he become an 'incomparable' image; nor is it possible through the dissimilar or the lesser or the subordinate that the true and archetypal and greater and self-determining and incomparable might be shown; nor again through the creature can the natural form of the creator be understood. For indeed no other nature demonstrates the other within itself. But even the Father is found to have become without subsistence, when the heretics do not teach the character.

Not of his hypostasis. But even the invisible, uncomposed, and formless God does not possess an image such as those they claim is imitative. And he clearly dissolves their argument and their induction, saying: 'To be equal to God was not considered a robbery.' And Moses also leads forward concerning a natural image, saying thus: 'Adam begat Seth according to his image' (Gen 5:3). Yet Seth was not necessarily of a different substance from Adam, yet he called the image and likeness of the essence an 'idea'.

But also concerning man, he says, it has been written, that he is 'an image and glory of God'. But nowhere, O you [ones], has it been written that man or any other creature is to be 'an emanation of the glory of God and a character of the hypostasis'. It is something else to be a man as an image of God, that is, the thing made of the maker, just as Solomon says concerning the product of a carpenter: 'The maker is perceived in a likeness to the things created'; but it is something else to be, according to the same form and identical and co-ruling, an emanation of glory and a character of hypostasis, in-dwelling and unerring. For he says: 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). But he who has seen a man has not seen God, just as he who has seen the product has not seen the carpenter.

But it is also necessary that for the only invisible God, that image is to be only invisible, and not the visible man according to the image. Therefore, the Son is not like any other: for he writes, 'Who shall be conformed to the Lord?' (Rom 8:29). Nor is he unlike his own Father: 'For I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), he says. And those who take the concept of the creator's image upon him, they resemble Nebuchadnezzar, worshipping an unconscious image made by [someone].

And God justly cast out Adam through the disobedience from the paradise; but the Son brought in the thief, and Adam with him, and the whole common race, as being altogether equal in divinity and goodness and lordship to the one who cast [them] out. Where has it been written that 'the Father is incomparable' to his own Only-begotten? Or that his Son is the creator and judge of all, according to his divine nature and the infinite nature of all things removed from them, is a 'creature'? Or altogether that at no time 'he was' (John 1:1)? Or where did the Father say privately, 'Create a son for me,' or the Son [say]?

title: Refutation of the Error regarding the Devil and the Trinity
english: "Was he created by the Father?" (16.53) Such a thing is terrible to hear and to say, and is to be avoided. 16.54 Truly, such things are found nowhere at all in the divine and spiritual scripture; on the contrary, when comparing himself to the Father, all the words concerning the divinity of the Only-begotten are found, showing him to be one with himself and of the same essence. 16.55 But no child, or infant, or offspring is ever spoken of regarding the eternal generation from above, which cannot be characterized at all, so that no one might imagine a small or subtle meaning in those previously sophistical blasphemies, but rather [he is] Son because of his perfection, his being unoriginated, and being inseparably of the same nature as the Father. 16.56 All things that are considered by some to be small regarding divinity, such as "the one who sent me is greater than I" (John 14:28) due to his philanthropic and ineffable humanity which came through us and for us, are used by the holy books. 16.57 Because of this, it is written that angels are made less, according to the apostle: "we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, through the suffering of death" (Hebrews 2:9). 16.58 I think, though I am not entirely certain, that regarding the Father and himself, he spoke showing the goodness and consubstantiality of both: "either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for from the fruit" (Matthew 12:33), he says, "the tree is known."

17.1 Since those who fight against God dare to say that those with the Son and the Holy Spirit are the first creation, while Macedonius says only the Spirit, the weight of remembering such rejected and condemned sayings would fall upon the holy and consubstantial Trinity. 17.2 We will show, setting forth the divine scriptures, how the first creation of God came to be: a first creation, exalted from the heavens, was cast down like lightning, as the Creator himself saw it well and later justly cast it down in the Gospel. 17.3 He says thus according to Job: "But behold, a beast beside you eats grass like oxen; behold, its strength is in its loins, and its power is on its belly. It set its tail like a plume..." (Job 40:15).
...his nerves are woven together, his ribs are bronze, and his back is an iron vessel. This is a beginning of a creation of the Lord made to be played with by the angels.

17.4 So he makes himself to say that the devil is a first creation, being played with by the holy angels because of his unrighteousness and the evilness of his will. But the Son, having created even this one, would not, nor indeed was the Spirit of God created.

18. Concerning the Holy Trinity and that because of the sameness of essence the same names are called on both sides of the hypostases, except for the fatherhood, sonship, and the procession of the Spirit. For this is proper to each hypostasis individually. And that at times the Father, at times the Son, at times the Spirit will be preferred. And that both the triadic and the monadic is shown in the Scripture.

18.1 Therefore, from all the things said, it has been established that those things turn out to be entirely foreign to the truth. For to find things out through cleverness is the work of sophistry, but wisdom is to investigate the Scriptures with reverence and with an appropriate reception.

18.2 It is necessary, therefore, having passed over their improbable sophistries and disputes, to wash the salty things with the intelligible water of the Holy Spirit—that is to say, to show having uncovered the ears—that the Scriptures, because of the sameness of divinity, at times name one of the divine hypostases, and at times name the three, and to each of them they similarly grant the good,

18.3 as when Moses says: 'Hear, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one' (Deut 6:4), in order to say 'one' declaring the one divinity, but through 'Lord', then 'God' and again 'Lord' signifying the Trinity, by which all cosmic and super-cosmic good has been and will be for men; and again: 'God said, let there be an expanse, and God made the expanse, and God saw that it was good' (Gen 1:6-10); it should be noted that he also names three hypostases and names each one God, and shows the harmony and the cooperation of the one speaking, the one making, and the one praising.
18.4 And again: 'God stands as protector,' he says, 'speaking to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons: thus you shall bless Israel;...'
